full_judgment: 26. The next important witness on whom the trial Court relied is P.W. 2 M.S. Molla and admittedly he is an officer of the Customs Department working at the Zia International Air Porl. He deposed that on 30.5.88 at 11 A.M: the baggage’s of the appellant were placed for examination at the crews counter and those were placed in presence of Safiar Rahman (who is a material witness and we draw adverse inference against the prosecution for withholding him without any reason) and at that time he went there and they demanded baggage declaration form from the crew. He further deposed that they found the echo lac bag rather heavy and on being suspicious they took the appellant to the room of the Deputy Collector of Customs in whose presence the Echolac bag was .searched and they found gold bars in the pocket of the bag. He further deposed that the search was conducted in presence of the Deputy Collector of Customs Mr. Shahjad. Hossain who is a material witness and for withholding whom without any reason we draw adverse inference against the prosecution. P.W. 2. M.S. Moll a further deposed that he himself prepared the seizure list where the appellant put his signature. Appellant wrote that the gold bars do nor belong to him and that he does not know who had kept them. He says that the appellant himself identified his baggage’s, But P.W. 6 Mannaf and P.W. 7 Soheli stated that the appellant stated that the bag docs not belong to him. It is the definite case of the prosecution that the accused appellant carried the gold in an echolac bag and those were re- covered from that bag by the customs officials P.Ws. 1 and 2. We have already found that the evidence of P.W. 1 in this respect is not believable. It is the defence case that echolac bag in which the gold bars were found does not belong to the appellant. We found from the evidence of P.W. 1 and 2 that when- ever a passenger or a crew carry any baggage, the airline officials place baggage tag with it. This is done to identify the baggage of a particular crew or the passenger. Admittedly in flight No. B.G. 042 there were 12/13 crews all of whom came from Dubai and their baggage’s were placed before the customs officials for checking. Toe prosecution in such circumstances must prove that an echolac bag was found with the baggage’s and the bag which contained the gold bars belonged to the appellant and unless this is proved and established the appellant cannot be convicted and sentenced. P.W. 1 during cross- examination admitted that it is common practice and known to every body that the baggage tags have two parts. One part remains attached to the baggage and the other one remains with the passenger or the crew and the baggage’s are delivered after comparing both the parts of the tag. This is the system every where and that was introduced for proper identification of the baggage. Here in the present case before us P.W. 1 admitted that the echo lac bag had a baggage tag. Even P.W. 2 who allegedly searched the baggage of the appellant admitted that the echo lac bag within  which the gold was found had a baggage tag. So the evidence of these two witnesses is to the effect that the echolac bag had a baggage tag and that the appellant was also searched and all his belongings were seized by seizure list Ext. 5. This seizure list contained 46 items but in those 46 items we find no baggage tag. Now if the echolac bag had a baggage tag and if that bag actually belonged to the appellant and if he himself produced bag before the Customs Officer for checking the other part of the tag must have been with him. The Customs Officer failed to seize that baggage tag or recover it from the appellant and send both the baggage tags along with the bag to the trial Court to prove that the bag which contained the gold actually belong to the appellant. When there is specific denial by the defence that seized echolacbag docs not belong to the appellant, the prosecution has got to produce both the tags to prove that the bag belonged to the appellant. Furthermore P.W. 1 who is the informant himself admitted that such ccholac bags are available in the market. In such circumstances it was the duty of the prosecution to prove that the seized echolac bag actually belonged to the appellant. But here the Customs officials though seized the en- tire contents of the bag and they also arrested the appellant they have not seized the baggage tag for connecting the accused appellant with the echo lac bag from which the gold bars were recovered. If it is a fact that the echolac bag belonged to the appellant and that it contained the baggage tag, the non-seizure of the baggage tag along with the echolac bag is a de- liberate act on the part of the Customs officer for keeping a gap in the continuity of events and that has been done with intention. Since tag or tags of the bag were seized, •the normal presumption is that there were no tags attached to the bag to show that the bag belonged to the appellant.We have already found that P.W. 1 gave contradictory statement and P.W. 2 who prepared the seizure list and who conducted the search has not seized the baggage tag to prove conclusively that the bag belonged to the appellant. This may have been done with ulterior motive. These witnesses failed to prove that the seized bag actually belonged to the appellant.
